newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy legislature will end when reforms over-Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Italy legislature will end when reforms over-Prodi.

text.p: Italian Prime Minsiter Romano Prodi said in an interview to be published on Thursday that the current parliament's term would end when the process of institutional reform had been completed.

"I had said I would lead a government for a full term. Well, it's clear that the institutional reform process closes the legislature. That is the way it is, by definition," Prodi told Sette magazine in an interview, according to an advance copy.

Italy has embarked on a lengthy process to reform its institutions and constitution to try to end its history of weak and ineffectual government. Prodi's government, in office since May 1996, is the 55th since World War Two.

A special parliamentary commission last week completed a five-point plan of draft changes involving a bigger role for an elected president, an updated constitution, smaller houses of parliament and some judicial reforms.

The draft is likely to meet a torrent of amendments when it goes to parliament, where changes have to be approved twice by both houses. Reforms would then be put to a referendum, meaning the whole process is unlikely to end until 1999 at the earliest.
Sette quoted Prodi as saying he welcomed the reform process. "May it come as soon as possible, even if that means ending the experience of government."
